To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we found that the adjuvant AS01 induced a rapid innate immune response, and we found that a gene signature previously associated with the efficacy of another AS01-adjuvanted vaccine was also associated with the immunogenicity of M72/ AS01 in the present study, which suggests that this gene signature may be associated with vaccine efficacy.
we have identified optimal postvaccinations time points for identifying peripheral blood transcriptome responses to the candidate tuberculosis vaccine, M72/AS1.

the adjuvanted recombinant protein candidate tuberculosis vaccine M/72AS01 induced a rapid innate immune activation in both WB and PBMCs, and that the optimal postvaccinational time points for identifying clinically relevant transcriptome changes in WB samples were 7, 14, or 17 days after vaccination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of time points for the evaluation of transcriptomic profiles in relation to immunogenicity and potentially protective efficacy of a candidate TB vaccine.
the identification of optimal postvaccinational time points for the evaluation of peripheral blood RNA expression changes in response to vaccination with M72/ASO1.
the development of novel adjuvant formulations and candidate TB vaccines, and the identification of biomarkers that can predict immunogenicity and efficacy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

1 day postvaccination is optimal for identifying early innate immune responses in PBMCs, while 7 to 17 days after vaccination is optimal for identifying potentially clinically meaningful transcriptomic changes in WB.
the optimal postvaccinated blood samples for transcriptome studies in relation to immunogenicity and efficacy would be PBMCs at day 14 and whole blood at day 7 postvaccination.
7, 14, or 17 days after the second dose is the optimal time point for measuring RNA expression in WB samples.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of systems biology to study vaccine immunogenicity is a promising approach.

a gene signature associated with protective efficacy of the malaria vaccine was also associated with M72/AS02 immunogenicity and could be identified at 10 days postvaccine administration in WB samples.

the use of a gene signature associated with vaccine efficacy and a blood transcription module approach allowed the identification of optimal postvaccinaton time points for evaluating RNA expression changes in WB samples.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the RNA expression profiles in WB and PB MCs are similar, and that the RNA expression profile in PBMCs is more informative than that in WB.

the use of a previously identified gene expression signature associated with the efficacy of another AS01-adjuvanted vaccine in the same study population can help identify optimal time points for assessing transcriptome responses to a vaccine candidate in a subsequent trial.
the RNA expression profiles in PBMCs and WB can be utilized to identify time points for optimal evaluation of the vaccine immunogenicity.
